meta.title: Who really said "In the struggle for survival, the fittest win out at the expense of their rivals because they succeed in adapting themselves best to their environment"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Darwin never wrote this line. Quote Investigator and Cambridge's Darwin Correspondence Project trace it to a 1962 history textbook's summary of his ideas.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In the struggle for survival, the fittest win out at the expense of their rivals because they succeed in adapting themselves best to their environment'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Darwin. It began as a textbook's paraphrase of his ideas in 'Civilization Past and Present' (1962) and was later mis-credited to him.

answer.label: Not Charles Darwin — a 20th-century textbook paraphrase
answer.authorName: Textbook authors of “Civilization Past and Present”
answer.authorDates: T. Walter Wallbank, Alastair M. Taylor & Nels M. Bailkey · American historians · line first printed 1962
answer.sourceLine: Darwin never wrote or said this. Quote Investigator found the earliest instance in the 1962 edition of the history textbook “Civilization Past and Present” (p. 578), where the sentence was the authors’ own gloss on Darwin’s ideas — not a quotation from him. Cambridge’s Darwin Correspondence Project lists it among “Six things Darwin never said.” The line was mistaken for Darwin’s own words and was circulating under his name by 2006.

source.excerpt: In the struggle for survival, the fittest win out at the expense of their rivals because they succeed in adapting themselves best to their environment.
trail: 1962 — earliest known appearance, in the textbook “Civilization Past and Present” (p. 578), as the authors’ paraphrase of Darwin, per Quote Investigator.
1971 — quoted, still with attribution to the textbook, in Ritchie R. Ward’s The Living Clocks, from which it “escaped into the wild,” per the Darwin Correspondence Project.
By 2006 — the sentence was circulating directly under Darwin’s name, and by 2009 was being falsely sourced to On the Origin of Species, per Quote Investigator.
Cambridge scholars place it among the “Six things Darwin never said.”
source.excerptNote: As printed in “Civilization Past and Present” the sentence was the textbook authors’ summary of Darwin’s thinking — presented in their own voice, not as a quotation from Darwin.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording first appears in the 1962 edition of the U.S. college textbook “Civilization Past and Present,” so the sentence is a 1962-vintage text and remains in copyright in the United States as the work of its named authors and publisher. It is not a public-domain Darwin quotation — Darwin did not write it.

author.name: Charles Darwin
author.heading: About Charles Darwin
author.metaLine: 1809–1882 · English naturalist · author of On the Origin of Species
author.bio: Charles Robert Darwin was the English naturalist whose 1859 On the Origin of Species established evolution by natural selection. His actual prose is careful and hedged; he did not coin slogans about the “fittest” winning — the phrase “survival of the fittest” itself was Herbert Spencer’s, which Darwin only later adopted. Because his name is shorthand for evolution, tidy motivational lines summarizing his ideas are routinely pinned on him.

misattribution.heading: How Darwin got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Darwin” lines online, yet it is not his. It began life as a textbook’s tidy summary of natural selection and was gradually mistaken for a direct quotation.

items.why: Darwin wrote no such sentence. Quote Investigator found “no substantive evidence” that Darwin made the statement, and Cambridge’s Darwin Correspondence Project lists it among things “Darwin never said.”
Later posts claimed Darwin wrote the line in On the Origin of Species; he did not — the sentence appears nowhere in it, per Quote Investigator.

items.who: “It is not the strongest of the species that survives … the most adaptable”
items.why: That better-known (also non-Darwin) line traces to a 1963 talk by management professor Leon C. Megginson; it is a separate paraphrase and should not be conflated with the “fittest win out” sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author of the wording is the team behind the history textbook “Civilization Past and Present” (1962) — summarizing Darwin, not quoting him.

context.heading: Why it feels like Darwin
lead: The sentence captures the popular caricature of natural selection — competition, winners, adaptation — in one confident line, which is exactly why it reads as pure Darwin. But Darwin’s own writing is qualified and rarely sloganeering, and the crisp phrase “survival of the fittest” was Herbert Spencer’s coinage, not his.

The line is a textbook’s teaching gloss that lost its quotation marks. Once Darwin’s name attached to it, it spread through quote sites and social media faster than anyone stopped to check whether he ever wrote it.
context.pull: A textbook’s summary of Darwin, mistaken for Darwin himself.
